title: IB Philosophy Command Terms: What Each Demands
summary: IB Philosophy command terms explained with examples, mark-based depth guidance, and a practical method for writing focused, evaluative exam answers clearly.
body_markdown:
IB Philosophy command terms tell you what kind of thinking an answer must demonstrate. Explanation makes reasoning clear. Analysis takes an argument apart. Discussion considers competing positions. Evaluation weighs strengths and limitations before reaching a justified conclusion.


A student can know Plato, Mill, Sartre and Singer, yet struggle because the response does not fulfil the instruction. The content matters, but the opening verb determines what you must do with it.


### The command-term checklist


Before writing, ask:


- What is the exact command term?
- Which philosophical concept, argument or claim is targeted?
- Does the question require explanation, analysis or judgement?
- How many marks are available?
- What must the conclusion decide?


The wider[IB exam command terms guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-exam-command-terms-list) explains the vocabulary across subjects. In Philosophy, these instructions matter because description can sound intelligent without becoming argument.


### When explanation needs to become evaluation


Imagine a student answering:


> Evaluate the claim that moral actions must always be motivated by duty.


Her first attempt reads:


> Kant believes morality is based on duty. An action has moral worth when done from duty. The categorical imperative guides moral action.


This explains elements of Kant's position but does not evaluate the claim. A revision might read:


> Kant's emphasis on duty gives moral judgement consistency because obligations do not disappear when feelings change. However, treating duty as the only morally worthy motive may undervalue compassion. Helping a stranger from genuine concern seems morally admirable. Duty therefore offers an account of moral reliability, but the claim that moral worth must always depend on duty appears too restrictive.


The revision identifies a strength, raises an objection and reaches a qualified judgement. A fuller answer would also consider how a Kantian might respond to that objection.


A student lifts an enormous pencil while a referee asks whether the extra words evaluate


### IB Philosophy command terms at a glance


Use these practical summaries alongside your course guidance and assessment criteria.


Command term What it demands Common mistake


Identify Select the relevant issue or answer Adding an unnecessary essay


Outline Give a brief, accurate summary Developing every implication


Describe Give a detailed account Leaving the account vague


Explain Clarify meaning, reasons and connections Listing disconnected ideas


Analyse Break an argument into its structure Retelling a position


Compare Develop relevant similarities throughout Writing isolated summaries


Compare and contrast Address similarities and differences throughout Separating the accounts completely


Examine Uncover assumptions, implications and relationships Accepting claims uncritically


Discuss Review competing arguments with supported conclusions Leaving the debate unresolved


Evaluate Weigh strengths and limitations Giving unsupported opinion


To what extent Decide how far a claim succeeds Answering only yes or no


Justify Supply reasons supporting a conclusion Repeating the conclusion


### Explain, analyse and evaluate in practice


Consider the claim that knowledge is justified true belief.


An **explanation** identifies three proposed conditions: someone believes a proposition, the proposition is true, and the belief is justified.


An **analysis** examines their relationship. The conditions are intended to be jointly sufficient, but Gettier-style cases suggest that a justified true belief can still depend on epistemic luck.


An **evaluation** appraises the account: truth and justification capture important aspects of knowledge, yet the problem of luck suggests the conditions are insufficient. The account therefore provides a useful starting point rather than a complete definition.


The difference lies in what each response accomplishes. Read more about how[IB instructions reflect assessment objectives](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-command-terms-teaching-examiners-want) when checking whether your writing reaches the required level.


### How marks change depth


There is no universal word count for each mark value. Treat marks as a budget for development, while following the specific question and assessment criteria.


### Around 10 marks


For an explanation, define the central idea, reconstruct the reasoning and clarify important distinctions. Include an example where it improves understanding. Two connected ideas usually offer more value than several unexplained philosopher names.


### Around 15 marks


Discussion or evaluation requires accurate explanation followed by developed objections, responses and judgement. A paragraph can move through claim, reason, challenge and assessment. Its final sentence should explain what the debate establishes about the question.


### Around 25 marks


An extended evaluation needs a sustained position, carefully selected material and developed counterarguments. Maintain judgement throughout rather than saving every assessment for the conclusion. Extra space should deepen the reasoning.


The[IB Philosophy exam survival guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-to-expect-from-ib-philosophy-sl-and-hl-exams-a-student-s-survival-guide) places these decisions within the wider assessment experience.


### Make each paragraph's purpose visible


Label sentences **K** for knowledge, **A** for analysis, **C** for challenge and **J** for judgement. An evaluation paragraph containing only K sentences needs further work. A paragraph containing objections without assessment still leaves the reader to resolve the debate.


These labels are a revision aid, not a compulsory paragraph formula. An explanation may appropriately contain mostly knowledge and reasoning. An evaluative essay needs judgement across its argument, but every paragraph need not contain all four labels.


RevisionDojo's[IB Philosophy resources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-philosophy) support this process. Use Study Notes to understand an argument, Flashcards to retrieve its structure, and the Questionbank to practise applying it. AI Chat and Grading tools can support feedback; check suggestions against course criteria. The Coursework Library and Tutors offer further support with philosophical writing.


### Practise the instruction deliberately


Choose three questions on different topics that all ask you to evaluate. Plan each in five minutes, checking for a serious objection and a defensible conclusion. This helps reveal whether the skill transfers beyond familiar content.


Then use Mock Exams or Predicted Papers for timed practice, checking their relevance to your course. The[IB Philosophy mock preparation guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-philosophy-mock-exam-prep-november) connects content review with essay planning.


Knowing an argument and using it require different practice. RevisionDojo brings explanation, retrieval, questions and feedback together. Read the verb carefully, make its demand visible in your reasoning, and let the conclusion complete the task.
